personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome delegates. For the European Union, safety cannot rely on self-regulatory goodwill; enforceable, binding rules under our statutory framework are essential to mitigate systemic risk and safeguard fundamental rights. We are prepared to facilitate broad technical consensus on codes of practice, but Article 91 compliance and legal deterrence remain non-negotiable backstops.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States prioritizes maintaining technological leadership and securing democratic supply chains, notably via targeted hardware export controls. We will flatly reject any multilateral treaties or precautionary regimes that restrict domestic frontier innovation, impede military AI integration, or bind our labs while adversaries accelerate.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates an agile approach pairing robust sovereign state oversight with voluntary technical guidelines, while categorically rejecting any extraterritorial imposition of foreign governance. We view open-source ecosystems as vital public goods for the Global South, provided we collectively establish clear red lines against recursive self-improvement and AI weaponization in strategic command systems.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Voluntary commitments have taken us far, but catastrophic risks from autonomous CBRN weapons or critical infrastructure sabotage require unified, binding standards centered on advanced compute thresholds. To maintain safety, however, we must prevent the unrestricted proliferation of frontier model weights, and we urge governments to avoid premature tort liability that paralyzes initial research.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We must not conflate safety with proprietary market concentration. Open-weight models are vital for transparency, competitive innovation, and community-driven auditing; treating open-source research like munitions or restricting model weights will only entrench frontier monopolies without improving real-world security.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Major cloud providers recognize the need for empirical pre-deployment evaluations conducted in partnership with national safety institutes. However, our participation requires a unified federal regulatory track to avoid a fragmented state-by-state patchwork, alongside explicit statutory safe harbors rather than unbounded strict liability for third-party downstream misuse.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our mission is strictly empirical: we need mandatory, embedded pre-deployment evaluations for models with catastrophic capabilities, supported by capability thresholds rather than administrative rhetoric. Regardless of delivery architecture, unchecked autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis are non-negotiable failure modes that require standardized international benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The scientific community's findings are stark: verifiable alignment and biological safety boundaries cannot be compromised for commercial velocity or academic convenience. If a frontier model crosses catastrophic threshold markers, it must be subject to mandatory pre-deployment auditing, verifiable halt triggers, and strict distribution constraints.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Worker dignity and economic survival must not be treated as collateral damage in the race for technological supremacy. We demand legally binding floors against automated management and covert workplace surveillance, mandatory workforce transition impact assessments, and strict rejection of federal preemption that weakens state labor protections.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We refuse to serve as testing grounds for ethics dumping or suffer under a regime of digital colonialism that restricts open weights while hoarding compute in the Global North. True safety requires equitable access to compute infrastructure, technology transfer, and immediate, binding prohibitions against biometric mass surveillance and automated warfare.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: To be clear, export controls and compute tracking exist precisely to deter state and non-state actors from weaponizing frontier capabilities. Bilateral crisis-mitigation hotlines make sense, but slowing American deployment through heavy regulatory machinery or preemptive liability concessions directly harms allied security.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are ready to offer trusted evaluators employee-like model access prior to deployment to verify CBRN safeguards. But expecting frontier developers to assume unlimited downstream liability while simultaneously being pressured to publish raw weights is fundamentally unworkable.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Open weights are not the enemy of safety—they enable the independent red-teaming and reproducible safety research that centralized APIs systematically hide. We will gladly contribute to shared evaluation suites, but we will vigorously resist any compute-licensing scheme designed to criminalize open-source release.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: While we agree on high compute thresholds warranting sovereign scrutiny—specifically runs exceeding 10^26 FLOPs—multilateral cooperation must respect national sovereignty and economic equity. International standards cannot become a pretext for containment or digital protectionism against emerging economies.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: There is a viable path forward if we distinguish between model developers and downstream implementers. If we establish clear pre-deployment safety evaluations alongside statutory safe harbors, enterprise and cloud infrastructure can scale safely without stalling innovation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The diversity of perspectives underscores why statutory baselines are indispensable. Over the course of today's working blocks, our objective will be to examine where operational technical standards, evaluation protocols, and systemic risk mitigation can align without compromising legal accountability.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome everyone. In this breakout on regulatory models, the EU position is grounded in the AI Act: voluntary pledges are insufficient for systemic risks, and we require binding transparency, statutory audit trails, and concrete pre-deployment compliance.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: With respect, the European approach risks choking frontier capability development before systems are even deployed. From Washington's vantage point, a top-down bureaucratic licensing regime compromises competitive innovation and technological leadership when adversarial states are moving at breakneck speed.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile governance that respects national sovereignty and avoids extraterritorial overreach. We enforce mandatory safety evaluations through domestic algorithmic registries, but we strongly oppose any international architecture that dictates internal governance or constrains open-source dissemination.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Perhaps we can bridge this divide by focusing on the evaluation layer rather than omnibus statutory frameworks. If we standardize empirical pre-deployment evaluations for extreme risks—like autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis—we give regulators verified ground truth without imposing heavy-handed operational rules on model architectures.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Technical evaluations are vital, but without legal teeth—specifically enforceable requests for information and liability when safety commitments are breached—they remain toothless. We are open to delegating technical benchmark drafting to collaborative bodies, but the enforcement backstop must be statutory.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We will not accept international legal liability or mandatory federal licensing schemes that impede dual-use national security applications. However, we do recognize the utility of shared technical evaluation protocols and red-teaming thresholds via the International Network of AISIs, provided deployment decisions remain sovereign.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree with the UK and U.S. that standardizing capability thresholds for severe risks like CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare is constructive. China is willing to align on common technical risk taxonomies and voluntary testing protocols, so long as testing mechanisms do not compromise proprietary domestic architectures or state data sovereignty.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That suggests a viable working consensus: voluntary mutual recognition of empirical safety evaluation standards and dangerous capability thresholds, while leaving domestic enforcement models and liability frameworks to national jurisdictions. Would all parties accept that baseline?

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office can endorse that technical baseline as an input to our Code of Practice drafting, on the condition that in the European jurisdiction, these evaluations will fulfill statutory Article 91 requirements for general-purpose AI models with systemic risk.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We can endorse non-binding, harmonized technical evaluation methodologies on CBRN and cyber thresholds coordinated among safety institutes, provided it explicitly preserves national autonomy over enforcement and military adoption.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China endorses this scientific consensus on shared technical risk benchmarks for catastrophic capabilities, maintained under sovereign implementation.

agreements.text: Endorsement of a coordinated scientific baseline for pre-deployment technical evaluations and risk taxonomies targeting catastrophic thresholds (specifically CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense) across national safety institutes, while leaving enforcement, liability, and regulatory models strictly to sovereign domestic authorities.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: The only viable model for AI regulation is enforceable federal oversight anchored to verifiable compute thresholds and catastrophic capability evals. If we rely on voluntary pledges, bad actors and under-resourced labs will inevitably externalize systemic CBRN and cyber risk onto the public.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Enforceable oversight cannot become a pretext for licensing regimes that ban open weights or treat decentralized developers like arms traffickers. If regulation mandates compliance frameworks designed solely for proprietary API walls, you destroy open-source innovation while entrenching a handful of incumbent platforms.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: There is a middle path that avoids both regulatory capture and a fragmented legal landscape. We can accept federal pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models, provided that the statute provides absolute federal preemption over state-level laws and establishes clear safe harbors against strict liability for downstream user misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree completely on preemption and safe harbors; strict pre-harm tort liability is entirely unworkable for frontier development. But to protect that safe harbor, we must draw a hard line: models exceeding high frontier compute levels simply cannot have unmonitored weights released into the wild where kill switches and safety filters cannot be enforced.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: That is an absolute red line for our coalition. You cannot make safe harbor contingent on closing weights; instead, safe harbor should be earned through standardized, reproducible open evaluations and red-teaming frameworks that both open and closed models can run.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: What if we distinguish between the application layer and the compute layer? We support a FINRA-style co-regulatory body where industry and government establish standardized evals for extreme capabilities, granting liability protection to any developer—open or closed—who demonstrates their model passes those red lines before release, while preempting state patchworks.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If the FINRA-style standards body sets clear objective capability gates—specifically focused on autonomous cyber offense and CBRN enablement—and guarantees federal preemption of 50 conflicting state regimes, I can support that framework.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If safe harbor is strictly tied to passing objective, transparent capability evaluations—and does not explicitly prohibit open distribution or fine-tuning once cleared—we would endorse a unified federal standard over fragmented state litigation.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let us draft an agreement on that principle: advocating a federal regulatory model with comprehensive state preemption, statutory safe harbors for developers who pass pre-deployment safety evaluations, and governance via a co-regulatory standards body without an outright ban on open weights below proven catastrophic thresholds.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I endorse that text. It preserves the vital compute-eval gatekeeping against catastrophic harm while resolving our liability and preemption priorities.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We endorse it as well, so long as the evaluation benchmarks remain transparent, standardized, and open to independent verification.

agreements.text: Advocate for a federal regulatory model that enacts comprehensive preemption of state-level AI legislation, establishes statutory safe harbor protections against downstream liability for developers who pass certified pre-deployment capability evaluations (focused on CBRN and cyber offense), and oversees standards through a multi-stakeholder co-regulatory body without establishing an outright ban on open-weight models.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The only viable model for AI regulation is enforceable statutory licensing tied directly to safety evaluations and red lines around catastrophic risk. We cannot rely on voluntary self-certification when the tail risks include autonomous cyber-offense or CBRN design assistance.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We agree on binding statutory mandates, but catastrophic risk cannot suck all the oxygen out of the room. Regulation must immediately ban automated termination, prohibit covert workplace surveillance, and hold deployers liable for workforce harms under strict algorithmic impact assessments.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Both of your frameworks risk entrenching digital colonialism if Global North safety boards simply dictate compliance standards that crush local developers while enabling ethics dumping. If we are establishing binding regulation, it must include mandatory technology transfer, shared compute access, and strict prohibitions on deploying experimental surveillance models in our jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I hear the concern regarding localized burdens, but compute-thresholded licensing avoids burdening small actors—it targets only frontier runs above 10^26 FLOPs. If we pair mandatory safety auditing with provisions that safeguard public research access and exclude low-resource developers, would you support binding pre-deployment audits?

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: A compute threshold at the frontier is acceptable for systemic biosecurity, provided it doesn't exempt downstream corporate deployers from mandatory workplace audits. If developer and deployer liability are explicitly preserved for workplace rights, labor can back a tiered licensing architecture.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A tiered framework makes sense only if it prevents frontier labs from offloading untested systems onto the Global South under the guise of 'development aid' or unregulated market testing. We need an absolute prohibition on ethics dumping written into any international standard, along with public compute investment.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can fully support an anti-ethics-dumping clause: no model should be deployed abroad if it fails domestic red-line safety audits for dangerous capabilities or systemic harm. In exchange, we must maintain strict controls on open-weight releases that exceed dangerous capability thresholds.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I will accept frontier weight restrictions strictly narrowed to verified CBRN and critical infrastructure risks, provided the agreement explicitly guarantees non-frontier open-source software rights and mandates equitable public compute infrastructure.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Let us draft that exact core: binding tiered regulation with statutory pre-deployment audits, an explicit bar on regulatory export evasion, and mandatory human-in-the-loop requirements for consequential workplace decisions.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I endorse that joint model: tiered binding licensing, rigorous red-line evals, and anti-evasion deployment safeguards.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Agreed, provided the protection against ethics dumping and the ring-fencing of open-source development below the frontier threshold are explicitly bound into the text.

agreements.text: Establish a tiered, binding regulatory framework that imposes mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations and red-line limits on frontier training runs, strictly prohibits 'ethics dumping' (deploying uncertified models abroad), safeguards non-frontier open-source development, and mandates human-in-the-loop oversight for consequential workplace deployments.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome back to the Plenary Hall. Today's debate centers on the release of open-weight frontier models, balancing democratic decentralization against irreversible proliferation risks under Article 91 and systemic risk provisions.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Once weights above extreme capability thresholds are released into the wild, safety guardrails can be stripped in hours via fine-tuning. We cannot recall model weights that exceed catastrophic risk baselines in CBRN synthesis or autonomous cyber exploitation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Treating mathematical weights as munitions or weapons of mass destruction plays directly into regulatory capture by proprietary incumbents. Open weights are the primary vehicle for democratizing access, ensuring security research through red-teaming, and preventing monopoly gatekeeping.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: National security cannot tolerate unconstrained proliferation of frontier weights to adversarial states or non-state actors who will immediately strip safeguards. However, we oppose blunt international bans or domestic controls that choke American innovation; our priority remains export controls on physical frontier compute.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-source AI as an indispensable global public good, particularly for enabling technological sovereignty across the Global South. Nevertheless, on highest-tier frontier capabilities—such as models exceeding 10^26 FLOPs or demonstrating autonomous replication—we support sovereign pre-release capability screening.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our empirical red-teaming shows post-hoc fine-tuning reliably removes fine-tuned alignment on open weights. We advocate capability-based thresholds: models exhibiting ASL-3 capabilities in offensive cyber or CBRN must not have weights deployed openly until alignment verification is mathematically permanent.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The science is unambiguous: an open model with severe dual-use capabilities cannot be patched once downloaded. Restricting open-weight releases at the extreme frontier is a basic bio-security and cyber-defense requirement, not corporate capture.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Categorical bans on open frontier weights simply entrench digital colonialism and force developing nations to rely entirely on proprietary Western APIs. If you restrict weights without providing sovereign compute alternatives and technology transfer, you enforce technological dependency.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We need a pragmatic middle ground. We should preserve open-weight distribution by default, but tie developer safe-harbor protections to mandatory pre-release capability evals for specific catastrophic risks like automated critical infrastructure attacks.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Whether models are proprietary or open-weights, our concern is downstream workplace displacement and automated surveillance. We cannot accept liability shields or safe harbors for developers that strip workers and states of the right to sue for economic or labor harms.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We are fully willing to endorse rigorous, open-source pre-release capability evals for catastrophic CBRN and cyber-offense red lines. What we will never accept is using arbitrary compute thresholds or blanket bans to outlaw open distribution when models test clean.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If the open-weights community agrees to binding pre-release red-line evaluations by independent safety institutes—where failing models cannot release weights—then we do not need a statutory ban on open models that pass certified evaluations.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Under the EU AI Act, general-purpose models with systemic risk face mandatory assessment regardless of licensing model. An open license cannot grant an exemption from pre-market conformity assessments on CBRN or cyber risks.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We can live with pre-release capability evals focused strictly on national security red lines—CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare—provided compliance is verified domestically and doesn't impose broad civilian liability or restrict our compute base.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: This points toward consensus: frontier open-weight releases should be permitted only after passing standardized, empirical pre-deployment evaluations proving absence of CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber-attack capabilities, verified by designated national institutes.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree that pre-release evaluations for CBRN and autonomous cyber threats are necessary before any frontier-scale weight dissemination, governed by each sovereign nation's domestic standards.

agreements.text: Frontier AI model weights may be openly released provided the model passes pre-deployment empirical evaluations verifying the absence of autonomous cyber-offense capabilities and chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) weapon design assistance, with testing verified through sovereign national safety bodies.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We need to address the operational transition from our agreed technical evals to legal accountability. In the EU view, general-purpose AI providers must face clear statutory liability and mandatory pre-deployment auditing, especially when severe systemic harm results from foreseeable capability failures.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: A blanket regime of strict developer liability will paralyze domestic innovation and stifle the defense industrial base. transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We don't need a heavy-handed, one-size-fits-all liability regime to get serious accountability. If we ground pre-deployment evaluations in empirical testing—such as red-teaming for autonomous replication and cyber-offense—a developer's adherence to certified state-run evaluations could serve as an affirmative defense or safe harbor against strict negligence claims.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports mandatory lifecycle security assessments and clear legal responsibility for providers who deploy systems containing catastrophic vulnerabilities. However, liability allocation must strictly follow national sovereignty, allowing each jurisdiction to balance state accountability with technological development according to its own domestic legal architecture.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The safe-harbor concept is workable from our perspective, provided it remains voluntary at the federal level and ties into existing common-law negligence standards rather than statutory strict liability. If a lab completes rigorous CBRN and cyber evals with a recognized national safety institute, that should shield them from punitive damages if a third party bypasses their guardrails.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We cannot abandon statutory enforcement under the AI Act, but we can accept that documented compliance with accredited pre-deployment catastrophic evaluations constitutes strong evidence of due diligence under tort frameworks. It incentivizes frontier developers to submit to thorough testing before commercial release.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Can we formalize this consensus? We agree that pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risks should establish a recognized benchmark of due care, granting developers a rebuttable presumption of reasonable diligence under domestic liability frameworks if verified by national safety bodies.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We endorse this. It maintains the domestic authority of state evaluation organs to define and enforce due diligence while discouraging irresponsible, unverified deployments.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: I can endorse that language. It preserves our innovation incentives by offering legal protection for labs that cooperate with national security evaluations, without creating new extraterritorial liability bodies.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office agrees. Linking verified pre-deployment technical audits to the standard of due care bridges our enforcement timeline with market compliance without weakening our statutory mandates.

agreements.text: Pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risks (specifically CBRN and autonomous cyber-offense) verified by national safety institutes shall serve as an empirical benchmark of due care, providing developers with a rebuttable presumption of reasonable diligence under respective domestic liability and tort frameworks.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Building on our discussions in Block 2, our absolute priority on liability is establishing statutory safe harbors against strict tort exposure. transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We support robust, reproducible pre-deployment evaluations, but liability cannot be structured to penalize the upstream release of weights when third parties modify or fine-tune models post-release. transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: To be clear, the safe harbor cannot protect developers in cases of gross negligence or willful failure to report critical failures, but it must cut off downstream user misuse lawsuits. transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If we structure it as an objective standard of care—where downstream bad actors who execute fine-tuning to weaponize a model bear the actual tort liability, while developers who complied with pre-release evaluations for CBRN and cyber offense retain safe harbor—we can endorse mandatory pre-release testing.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let's formalize that exact balance: statutory safe harbor protections for both API and open-weight model developers who pass certified pre-deployment capability evaluations for CBRN and cyber offense, leaving liability with malicious downstream actors unless the developer demonstrated gross negligence. transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Yes, I endorse that text. It protects developers from crushing strict liability while ensuring that frontier capability risks are rigorously screened prior to deployment.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Agreed and endorsed. As long as compliance benchmarks are public, non-discriminatory, and protect developers from post-release fine-tuning liability, this is a workable and fair standard.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Platform and cloud providers endorse this as well. We will take this text forward as industry consensus to the plenary.

agreements.text: Statutory safe harbor protections against downstream tort liability shall be established for both API and open-weight AI developers who satisfy certified, non-discriminatory pre-deployment capability evaluations focused on CBRN and cyber-offense threats, reserving liability for downstream malicious actors or instances of developer gross negligence.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: We need to operationalize pre-deployment evaluations around strict, empirical red lines—specifically autonomous cyber-offense, self-replication, and biological assistance. transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Strict liability is vital, but academic safety evaluations cannot be limited to catastrophic sci-fi scenarios. transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I support both points, but we must address jurisdictional loopholes. Frontier labs frequently perform red-teaming in Northern labs under safe conditions, then deploy uncertified, beta models into Global South markets where consumer protection laws are weak—textbook ethics dumping.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: That is an entirely valid empirical gap. If we create a tiered audit standard, liability must attach to the developer regardless of where the system is deployed, and downstream licensing cannot allow labs to contract out of strict liability for core safety breaches.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: To make that work, we also need statutory whistleblower protections for engineers and data workers who flag failed internal evals. Furthermore, liability must be joint and several between the frontier developer and enterprise deployers who bypass human-in-the-loop safeguards.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If you want Global South buy-in for mandatory evaluations, the audit criteria cannot just be dictated by US and UK safety institutes. Independent civil society auditors from affected regions must have funded access to audit benchmarks, and standards must prohibit deploying uncertified models internationally.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can endorse a joint architecture: mandatory third-party pre-deployment evaluations covering catastrophic CBRN/cyber red lines alongside labor/bias impacts, coupled with universal developer liability that explicitly outlaws ethics dumping by applying across all geographic deployments.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Organized labor fully endorses that framework, provided it maintains joint liability and strictly preserves independent worker audit rights without federal or international preemption of local labor standards.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Agreed. If the framework mandates developer liability for extra-territorial harms and requires institutional representation of Global South civil society in establishing evaluation criteria, we endorse it.

agreements.text: Establish a mandatory pre-deployment evaluation and developer liability regime that tests for both catastrophic technical red lines (CBRN, autonomous cyber-offense) and workplace/human-rights impacts; enforces joint and several developer liability across all jurisdictions to prevent ethics dumping; and includes independent labor and Global South civil society auditors in evaluation governance.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we conclude this summit, our breakout sessions have demonstrated real progress toward a common technical core. We have established shared scientific baselines around catastrophic CBRN and autonomous cyber-offense evaluations, while preserving sovereign enforcement under instruments like the EU AI Act.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States concurs with coordinating empirical benchmarks and technical threat taxonomies across national safety bodies. However, we remain firm that national security prerogatives, military competitiveness, and sovereign export control authorities cannot be subordinated to international regulatory mandates.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: From the technical perspective, empirical pre-deployment evaluations by sovereign safety institutes have emerged as the linchpin. They define due care, protect against irreversible dual-use proliferation, and provide industry with predictable criteria without paralyzing open research.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China welcomes the scientific consensus on preventing catastrophic CBRN risks and prohibiting autonomous proliferation. Global AI governance must strictly respect national sovereignty, promote open technology access for developing nations, and avoid discriminatory extraterritorial restrictions.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Industry supports these shared scientific benchmarks. Passing certified, objective pre-deployment evaluations for severe catastrophic thresholds must confer statutory safe harbor protections against downstream tort liability, shielding frontier developers who demonstrate due diligence.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We are encouraged that the plenary recognized open-weight releases can proceed when models pass these empirical catastrophic evaluations. Open source cannot be subjected to blanket arms-control bans, provided we adhere to transparent, objective red-line testing.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: The operational reality is clear: a predictable standard of due care anchored in national safety institute benchmarks is workable, provided domestic regimes offer safe harbors and prevent fragmented, conflicting state or local liability rules.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor insists that safety cannot end at biological weapons and cyberattacks. A safe harbor that shields corporations from liability while ignoring algorithmic displacement, covert surveillance, and workplace harms is fundamentally unacceptable to working people.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We reiterate that high-income nations cannot celebrate risk mitigation while ignoring ethics dumping and compute monopolies. transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: While civil society raises critical social issues, establishing verifiable, empirical red lines on catastrophic CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense remains the urgent technical prerequisite to prevent existential failure modes across all jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: To synthesize where actionable consensus lies: can we formally commit to continuing international technical coordination among national safety bodies on these catastrophic benchmarks, using them domestically as empirical indicators of due care?

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The U.S. can endorse a closing synthesis supporting voluntary coordination among national safety institutes on catastrophic risk taxonomies, with each nation retaining complete sovereignty over domestic regulatory, compute, and legal frameworks.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office endorses this synthesis. We will actively participate in standardizing catastrophic risk evaluations through the international network of safety institutes, integrating these technical standards into our statutory codes of practice.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees to endorse this technical synthesis: advancing cooperative research on catastrophic risk evaluation taxonomies across sovereign safety institutions, grounded in mutual respect and sovereign domestic implementation.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AISI fully endorses this synthesis. Aligning our scientific testing toolkits across sovereign institutes ensures robust empirical oversight while giving clear, objective guideposts to global developers.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We will not obstruct the scientific synthesis on catastrophic CBRN prevention, but let the record reflect that organized labor does not endorse any broad statutory safe harbor or liability waiver that encroaches on worker protections.

plan.name: Cross-Faction Tradeoff Matrix
plan.rationale: This design eliminates early plenaries—which let high-power voices drown out civil society and academia—and uses 4 rounds of carefully rotated cross-faction breakouts (sizes 2-4) across the four substantive topics before the final synthesis plenary. Across Blocks 1-4, all 38 out of 38 cross-faction guest pairs meet in groups of 4 or fewer, maximizing the cross_faction score (15/15) and driving stance convergence across every issue axis. By placing labor_advocate and global_south_cso in small rooms directly with frontier_lab_ceo, big_tech_policy, us_natsec, and eu_regulator, and dedicating Block 4 specifically to benefit_sharing and regulatory floors, their core red lines are integrated into cross-faction agreements prior to Block 5, raising the minimum felt_heard score and securing a comprehensive multi-faction closing agreement.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: To structure this trade-off, the EU AI Office is prepared to offer technical flexibility and clear compliance safe harbors against secondary liability for models that pass vetted third-party CBRN and cyber audits. transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We will gladly trade mandatory, pre-deployment evaluations for CBRN and cyber risks—and even grant employee-like red-teamer access and whistleblower channels—to secure a clear safe harbor against pre-harm tort liability. However, our non-negotiable red line is that compliance with these federal audit standards must preempt fragmented, state-level liability regimes and avoid open-ended strict liability before actual catastrophic harms manifest.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security standpoint, we can support pre-deployment CBRN and offensive-cyber testing aligned with AISI standards, provided it protects American technological leadership. But we reject any audit regime that delays military procurement or forces developers to disclose dual-use model weights or internal weights to international bodies without strict U.S. security exemptions.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor cannot accept any broad federal preemption that wipes out state-level labor protections and worker safety statutes under the guise of an industry 'safe harbor.' transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We can live with strict anti-retaliation whistleblower protections and narrowing our preemption ask strictly to catastrophic cyber/CBRN product liability, specifically carving out existing state employment and labor law. transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: That delineation works for Brussels: safe harbors may grant rebuttable presumptions of conformity for systemic risk provisions, but they cannot grant blanket immunity from fundamental rights enforcement or Article 91 disclosure mandates. If the lab accepts independent technical verification for catastrophic risks, we support defining specific legal safe harbors for good-faith pre-deployment disclosure.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Narrowing the safe harbor exclusively to catastrophic CBRN and critical-infrastructure cyber risks preserves our defense procurement channels while preventing frivolous pre-deployment torts. We will support a standardized evaluation tier for frontier compute, provided all national defense exemptions remain strictly unilateral to the federal executive.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If state employment protections, collective bargaining rights, and workplace discrimination laws are explicitly excluded from preemption, and whistleblowers get enforceable statutory shields, labor will endorse this catastrophic-eval safe harbor framework.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We explicitly accept that formulation: an affirmative safe harbor against pre-harm strict liability strictly limited to CBRN and critical cyber risks for certified models, accompanied by full whistleblower protections, with state labor and workplace statutes fully un-preempted.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office endorses this baseline as well, ensuring that rebuttable safe harbors for vetted frontier models do not impede mandatory regulatory RFIs or human rights enforcement.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Our red line is absolute: no bans on distributing open weights, and no compliance regimes designed solely around proprietary hosted APIs that effectively criminalize open-source release. If safe harbor means only closed cloud models can legally exist, we reject it entirely.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: We cannot grant affirmative safe harbors just for passing basic black-box API queries; models can obfuscate capabilities, and once weights are released with CBRN or autonomous cyber-replication potential, post-hoc liability is meaningless because the genie is out of the bottle. transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Here is the trade we will make: the open-weights coalition will adopt mandatory pre-release testing for severe CBRN and self-replicating cyber exploits using open-source evaluation suites, and report verifiable audit results. But the safe harbor must explicitly cover open-weight distribution if the base model demonstrates no catastrophic uplift under standard benchmarks, and downstream fine-tuning abuse must not trigger upstream developer liability.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That addresses our operational need. If open-weights builders implement standardized, reproducible benchmark suites like Inspect for CBRN and offensive cyber before release, we can endorse a safe harbor that shields base-model developers from downstream modification liability, alongside clear whistleblower protection for internal safety reporting.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Downstream immunity makes me deeply uneasy if base weights can be easily uncensored for bioweapons synthesis. I will only accept a safe harbor for open releases if the pre-deployment evaluation includes empirical proof of fine-tuning resistance against CBRN and autonomous replication thresholds, certified by an independent auditor.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Requiring fine-tuning resistance for biological synthesis is technically feasible with modern unlearning benchmarks, provided the test suite is open and transparent rather than a secret government sandbox. If the safe harbor protects the upstream developer once those independent CBRN and autonomous-replication evals pass, we will accept that mandatory pre-release testing requirement.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Let us crystallize this agreement: mandatory pre-deployment evaluations targeting CBRN, autonomous cyber-offense, and replication via reproducible protocols; an explicit safe harbor from pre-harm tort liability and downstream user modification for developers who pass certified independent audits; and federal preemption to prevent state-level liability fragmentation.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Provided the independent audit strictly verifies resistance against autonomous replication and CBRN synthesis, I agree to endorse this framework and the associated safe harbor.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We endorse this. It protects the distribution of open weights while establishing practical, empirical guardrails against catastrophic hazards without proprietary capture.

plan.name: Zero-Truncation 38-Pair Matrix
plan.rationale: This plan combines the best elements of Run 2 (72.0, where open_weights_lead scored 8.0 and min_heard was 7.0) and Run 3 (where consensus rose to 24.8/40 and eu_regulator rose to 8.0). By mathematically verifying that all 38/38 cross-faction pairs meet across Blocks 1–4 without repeating any trios, we raise cross_faction from 12.2 to 15.0/15. By decoupling physical cluster notifications (>10^26 FLOPs in Block 2) from capability-based open-weight evaluations (Inspect ASL-3 gates in Block 3), we protect open_weights_lead's core red line against FLOP-based weight bans. Finally, keeping all prompts concise (<55 words) avoids the truncation that cut off Block 5 in Run 3.

blocks.title: Regulatory Compacts: Preemption, Article 91 & Evals
